50 date-free ad mock-ups for the free live class

Prepared for Stephen, 26 October 2026. Nothing here is live: every ad needs your approval of the wording first.

Jump to the ads running now and how they're doing ↓

His copy blueprint, step by step (from his second video)

He takes his longest-running ad apart line by line. Every ad's main text now follows the same 10 steps, in Stephen's words and facts:

  1. A humble start, with specific details: no lessons, a battered street piano, songs worked out by ear (the story about each ad's own photo).
  2. The transformation: packed halls and crowds that fill city parks.
  3. The pivot to “one thing”: “I'm not telling you this to impress you… it came down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.”
  4. A line that might annoy people, plus their deepest wish: “This might annoy anyone who spent years on drills. But if you want to sit down and play the songs you love…”
  5. A real lesson inside the ad, against what they were told: “Most adults ask how to read music. Wrong question.” / “Talent isn't the difference. Order is.”
  6. Name exactly who it's for: “This is for you if…” (7 audiences).
  7. Say why what they tried failed: apps, YouTube and drills tell you which key to press next, not how the music is built.
  8. Proof that answers their biggest worry: too old → students started at 62 and 70; never played → John; tried before → Gary, “This is different!”.
  9. The method and the good news: “It's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes.”
  10. Bullets that tease (“What your left hand is actually for, and why nobody tells you”), then a soft, date-free call to action: “Tap Learn more to save your seat for the next live class.”

Plus his writing rules: 5th-grade reading level or below (ours: grade 3–5), short lines, about the reader, specific details, one theme per ad, first line opens a loop, a real student quote as the opener where we have one, curiosity + a specific benefit in the headline, positive over negative.

Open for you to decide: he also uses hard proof (awards, numbers). Our story ads leave out the Insider Weekly award and “40,000 students” (your call on 22 Oct). Say the word if you want them back in the proof step.

His hackBeforeNow

A1

Problem / reassuranceStreet pianoT1Top pick
Headline under the ad

Self-taught street pianist: your first song in ninety minutes

First line (what people see before “See more”)

I never had a single piano lesson. What I found instead changed everything.

Full ad text
I never had a single piano lesson. What I found instead changed everything.

I learned on a battered street piano, the kind people walk past every day. No teacher. No books. Just me, trying to work out how the songs I loved actually worked.

Then one day it clicked. Underneath almost every song there was something so simple I couldn't believe nobody had shown me first. Most people who "can't play" were never shown it. They were shown the drills.

I'm not telling you this to impress you. I'm telling you because all of it came down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This next part might annoy anyone who spent years on drills. But if you want to sit down at a piano and play the songs you love, by feel, for the people you love, it's true. Here goes:

Most adults ask, "How do I learn to read music?" Wrong question. The right one is, "How are the songs I love actually built?" Answer that, and reading becomes optional.

This is for you if you had lessons as a kid and quit. If you remember the exercise books, the drills, the teacher who sighed when you got it wrong. If you decided back then that you "just weren't musical" and you've carried that around ever since.

You were never the problem.

That's why most methods don't stick. They start with reading and exercises, and leave the music you love for "later". For most adults, later never comes.

Tried before and quit? So had Gary, whose verdict was simple: "This is different!" And if there's no piano in the house, don't worry. You don't need one to join the class.

The good news: I call it the Ridley Method, and I'm teaching it myself, live, for ninety minutes. No sheet music. No drills. Just the songs you love and the simple idea underneath them.

You'll see:

• The one idea that makes most songs suddenly make sense
• How to start a song you love in your very first session
• What to do with your left hand so it stops feeling useless
• Why the drills you did as a kid were the wrong place to start
• How ten minutes a day beats an hour you dread

It's free. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

Tap Learn more to save your seat for the next live class.

Play songs you love without reading a single note

Full ad text
Look closely at this photo. Nobody is reading music. Here's what they know instead.

There's a crowd around that piano and not one page of music in sight. Nobody's counting. Nobody's decoding notes. People are just hearing songs they love and singing along.

That's what most of us wanted when we first sat at a piano. Then lessons turned it into reading practice, and the music got pushed to "later". For most people, later never came.

Stephen Ridley taught himself on street pianos and now plays to packed halls and crowds that fill city parks. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he can do at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This might sound backwards. But if you want to be the one who sits down and plays when someone says "go on, play something", hear this:

Talent isn't what separates people who play from people who don't. Order is. People who start with songs keep going. People who start with drills quit.

This is for you if you've always wanted to play and never started.

Not because you didn't care, but because it always looked like years of practice before you'd play anything worth hearing. Something for "one day". It doesn't have to wait any longer.

That's why most methods don't stick. They start with reading and exercises, and leave the music you love for "later". For most adults, later never comes.

Never played at all? Neither had John. "I never played piano before in my life," John wrote. Now John plays a Roland keyboard and calls it "a blast".

The good news: it's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes. No sheet music. No drills. Just the songs you love and the simple idea underneath them.

What you'll learn:

• How a song you love is put together (you'll see it in minutes)
• Why some people can sit down and "just play"
• The mistake almost every adult beginner makes in week one
• How to practise ten minutes a day without it feeling like homework
• Why it's not too late, whatever your age

It's free. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

Simpler than it looks: play a song you love in ninety minutes

First line (what people see before “See more”)

It looks impossible from the outside. Here's the part nobody shows you.

Full ad text
It looks impossible from the outside. Here's the part nobody shows you.

From the outside it looks impossible. Two hands doing different things, no music in front of him, eyes closed half the time.

Up close it's much simpler. A few patterns, repeated in different songs. Learn those, a little at a time, and you'd be amazed how quickly your hands start doing things that looked impossible a month ago.

Stephen Ridley taught himself on street pianos and now plays to packed halls and crowds that fill city parks. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he can do at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

Here's the part most teachers won't say out loud. If you want to finally play the music you love instead of exercises, it matters more than anything else:

You don't need to practise more. You need to practise the right thing. Ten minutes on a song you love beats an hour of exercises you hate, every time.

This is for you if your days are already full. Work, family, everything else.

You don't have an hour a day to practise, and the good news is you don't need one. Stephen's students practise around ten minutes a day, on songs they actually like.

That's why most methods don't stick. They start with reading and exercises, and leave the music you love for "later". For most adults, later never comes.

Never played at all? Neither had John. "I never played piano before in my life," John wrote. Now John plays a Roland keyboard and calls it "a blast".

The good news: it's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes. No sheet music. No drills. Just the songs you love and the simple idea underneath them.

In the class you'll discover:

• What your left hand is actually for (and why nobody tells you)
• The simple pattern hiding inside most of the songs you love
• Why you don't need to read music to start
• How to play by feel, even if you were told you have no ear
• The ten-minutes-a-day habit that keeps adults going when lessons didn't

There's no cost and nothing to prepare. Just a pen, some paper, and the song you've always wished you could play.

The next live class is open now. Tap Learn more to pick your seat.

P1

PositivePositiveT2Top pick
Headline under the ad

Play your favourite song for your family this Christmas

First line (what people see before “See more”)

This Christmas, imagine being the one at the piano while everyone sings.

Full ad text
This Christmas, imagine being the one at the piano while everyone sings.

Imagine the room at Christmas. Everyone's there. Someone says, "Go on, play something."

And this year you sit down. You play the song you love, the one you always wished you could play, and the room goes quiet, then starts to sing. You don't need years of lessons for that moment. You need the right start, and a few weeks of ten minutes a day.

Stephen Ridley taught himself on street pianos and now plays to packed halls and crowds that fill city parks. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he can do at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This next part might annoy anyone who spent years on drills. But if you want to sit down at a piano and play the songs you love, by feel, for the people you love, it's true. Here goes:

Most adults ask, "How do I learn to read music?" Wrong question. The right one is, "How are the songs I love actually built?" Answer that, and reading becomes optional.

This is for you if there are grandchildren in your life, or soon will be.

Imagine them squeezed next to you on the piano bench while you play something they know, and them asking for it again. That's the kind of memory a child keeps for the rest of their life.

Apps, YouTube tutorials and years of drills all treat the symptom. They tell you which key to press next. None of them shows you how the music is built, so the moment the screen goes off, you're stuck.

Worried you're too old? Students have started at 62 and at 70. Marie, who started at 62, calls learning "a joy". Cyd, a retired college teacher who started at 70, calls the method "first rate".

The good news: it's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes. No sheet music. No drills. Just the songs you love and the simple idea underneath them.

You'll see:

• The one idea that makes most songs suddenly make sense
• How to start a song you love in your very first session
• What to do with your left hand so it stops feeling useless
• Why the drills you did as a kid were the wrong place to start
• How ten minutes a day beats an hour you dread

It's free. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

Headline under the ad

Skip the drills: play a song you love in ninety minutes

First line (what people see before “See more”)

When did piano stop being fun? For most people, the day the drills started.

Full ad text
When did piano stop being fun? For most people, the day the drills started.

Look at his face. That's what piano is supposed to feel like. Not dread before a lesson. Not counting out loud. Joy.

For most people, piano stopped being fun the day the drills started. The good news is it can be fun again from the very first session, if you start with music you love instead of exercises you don't.

Stephen Ridley taught himself on street pianos and now plays to packed halls and crowds that fill city parks. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he can do at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

This might sound backwards. But if you want to be the one who sits down and plays when someone says "go on, play something", hear this:

Talent isn't what separates people who play from people who don't. Order is. People who start with songs keep going. People who start with drills quit.

This is for you if you had lessons as a kid and quit. If you remember the exercise books, the drills, the teacher who sighed when you got it wrong. If you decided back then that you "just weren't musical" and you've carried that around ever since.

You were never the problem.

That's why most methods don't stick. They start with reading and exercises, and leave the music you love for "later". For most adults, later never comes.

Tried before and quit? So had Gary, whose verdict was simple: "This is different!" And if there's no piano in the house, don't worry. You don't need one to join the class.

The good news: it's called the Ridley Method, and Stephen is teaching it himself, live, for ninety minutes. No sheet music. No drills. Just the songs you love and the simple idea underneath them.

What you'll learn:

• How a song you love is put together (you'll see it in minutes)
• Why some people can sit down and "just play"
• The mistake almost every adult beginner makes in week one
• How to practise ten minutes a day without it feeling like homework
• Why it's not too late, whatever your age

It's free. You don't need a piano to join. Bring a pen, some paper and the one song you've always wanted to play.

Stephen Ridley taught himself on street pianos and now plays to packed halls and crowds that fill city parks. He'll tell you it was never about talent. Everything he can do at a piano comes down to one thing: understanding how songs are actually built.

What it tells us for the new ads

  1. No-text real photos win on what matters. The three ads using the plain concert-hall photo put 7.6–13.8 people in the room at the offer per $1,000; the designed cards 4.7–6.6. That's Sabri's “don't look like an ad”, proven in our own account, and it's why the new mock-ups are real photos with little or no design.
  2. But a photo needs a benefit in the headline, or it gets curiosity clicks that don't sign up (left-hand photo: 8% of visitors). The rewritten headlines fix exactly this.
  3. “Piano isn't hard, it's badly taught” is our proven line. It's on our best ad (Angle 3 LM) and our biggest (W2). Keep it in play; B2 and several mock-ups carry the same idea.
  4. Learn more beats Sign up on the outcome: same photo and headline, Learn more = 34.8% show-up and 13.8 at the offer per $1,000 vs 28.8% and 8.5. All mock-ups use Learn more.
  5. Every ad except the top five was starved: $8–$296 each. None of them was ever really tested, which is why new ads go into T1/T2 on their own budget.
  6. Act on this: keep Angle 3 LM (and let it have more budget), keep W2 as the control until a date-free winner replaces it, consider pausing 16S-P3 (lowest show-up and outcome). Your call: nothing has been changed.

Small print: “by ad name” misses sign-ups whose tag was lost (about 3%), and show-up for the 25 Oct class is final. Numbers under $1,000 of spend aren't shown per $1,000; they're too small.

A designed card that spells out the offer (live masterclass, day, time, “Save my seat”). That makes the click cheap to buy ($48 per 1,000 views) and the page converts best (20%), because people already know what they're signing up for. But it's the polished “middle” Sabri warns about, it has run since 16 Sep, and it puts only 6.6 people in the room at the offer per $1,000. Its image says “This Sunday 1 PM”, so it can't be date-free without a new version.

A real concert-hall photo with no text: it doesn't look like an ad, so it gets 5.6× W2's click rate and the cheapest visits ($1.31). But the headline (“Nobody ever told you what your left hand is for”) is pure curiosity, so only 8% of visitors register. Those who do are good: 29.7% show up. Fix = same photo, a headline with a specific benefit (what the mock-ups now do).
